title: Word Pattern
description: Brute force to optimized: rechecking every pair of positions versus two hash maps in a single pass.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Given a pattern string and a string s made of space separated words, determine whether s follows the exact same pattern, meaning there is a full bijection between each letter of pattern and each distinct word in s.

blocks.caption: Two hash maps, one per direction, verify the bijection between letters and words

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","pattern, a string of lowercase letters, and s, a string of space-separated lowercase words"],["Output","true if s follows pattern exactly, meaning a full bijection exists between letters and words, false otherwise"],["Goal","Verify this bijection efficiently, in a single pass rather than rechecking every pair of positions"],["Constraints","1 <= pattern.length <= 300, pattern consists of lowercase English letters, 1 <= s.length <= 3000, s consists of lowercase English letters and spaces"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["Every letter must map to exactly one word, and every word back to exactly one letter","A bijection check needs mapping consistency verified in both directions, not just one"],["Need to detect the first inconsistency as soon as it appears","Two hash maps, one per direction, checked and updated together in a single pass"],["Comparing every position against every other position","A direct lookup against a recorded mapping replaces an all-pairs recheck"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

Given a pattern string and a string s made of space separated words, determine whether s follows the exact same pattern, meaning there is a full bijection between each letter of pattern and each distinct word in s.

blocks.title: Analogy: Matching Nicknames to People, One to One
blocks.text: Like verifying that a coded message correctly assigns exactly one code letter per person, and exactly one person per code letter, with no code letter shared between two different people and no person given two different code letters.

blocks.caption: Every pattern letter must map to exactly one word, and every word back to exactly one letter

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: pattern = "abba", s = "dog cat cat dog"

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["a maps to \"dog\", b maps to \"cat\", consistently throughout","a genuine one to one match","Every occurrence of \"a\" lines up with \"dog\" and every occurrence of \"b\" lines up with \"cat\", in both directions, with no exceptions"],["Answer","true","The mapping between letters and words holds consistently at every position"]]}

blocks.text: Example: pattern = "abba", s = "dog cat cat fish"

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["The final \"a\" should map to \"dog\" again, but the word is \"fish\" instead","the mapping breaks","\"a\" was already recorded as mapping to \"dog\" at position 0, so seeing \"fish\" at a later \"a\" position contradicts that recorded mapping"],["Answer","false","A previously established letter-to-word mapping was contradicted"]]}

blocks.text: Edge case: pattern = "aaaa", s = "dog cat cat dog"
Every position in the pattern is the same letter "a", but the words are not all the same ("dog", "cat", "cat", "dog"), so a single letter cannot map to two different words, giving false.
5. How Should We Think?
Before comparing every position against every other, notice that "s follows pattern" is really a bijection question, and a bijection needs both directions checked, not just one.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: "s follows pattern" means two things simultaneously: every occurrence of the same letter in pattern must line up with the same word, and every occurrence of the same word in s must line up with the same letter.

Observation 2: Checking only the first direction, letter to word, would wrongly accept a case where two different letters happen to map to the same word, since that violates only the second direction.

Observation 3: A hash map from letter to word directly answers "what word must this letter map to" in O(1), and a second hash map from word to letter directly answers "what letter must this word map to" in O(1), together fully enforcing both directions of the bijection.

Observation 4: Scanning pattern and the split words together, position by position, and checking then recording both maps at each step means every conflict is caught the very first time it would occur, with no need to ever look back at earlier positions again.

Whenever a problem calls for a strict one-to-one correspondence between two sequences, maintain a hash map in each direction and check both at every position, since checking only one direction only enforces half the requirement.
This same two-map bijection check reappears in isomorphic-string style problems generally, anywhere "sequence A maps to sequence B, consistently and uniquely in both directions" needs to be verified.
6. Brute Force Solution
Split s into words, and for every position, check the mapping's consistency by rescanning every earlier position to verify no conflicting assignment exists, instead of using a direct lookup.
Step by step algorithm

items: Split s into a list of words, and check its length matches the pattern's length.
For each position, compare the current letter and word against every previous position's letter and word to check for a conflict.
If any conflict is found, the pattern does not match.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Both conditions, same pattern letter but different word, and different pattern letter but same word, are checked in the same inner loop, since either one alone represents a genuine violation of the required bijection.
The length check happens before any position-by-position comparison, since a length mismatch alone already guarantees no valid one-to-one correspondence can exist.
The inner loop compares position i against every position j, including positions before and after i, since without a saved mapping, there is no shortcut to know which other positions might conflict.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Every pair of positions is checked for a consistent mapping in both directions, so any genuine violation of the one to one correspondence is correctly detected.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), comparing every pair of positions.
Space: O(n), for the split list of words.

Limitation: checking every pair of positions is unnecessary. A direct hash map lookup can verify consistency for each new position in constant time by comparing it only against its recorded mapping, not every earlier position.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force rechecks the relationship between every pair of positions to catch a bijection violation, but a violation, when it exists, always involves comparing a position against something already established earlier, never something that has not been seen yet. That means the comparison does not actually need every other position, only "what was this letter, or word, already recorded as mapping to, if anything". Recording that mapping the first time a letter or word is seen, and checking against the recorded value on every later occurrence, replaces an all-pairs rescan with a single hash map lookup, since a hash map answers exactly the question "what did I already commit to for this key" in constant time.

Maintain two hash maps built in a single pass: one from pattern letter to word, and one from word to pattern letter. At each position, check whether the current letter is already mapped to a different word, or the current word is already mapped to a different letter; either case breaks the pattern. If no mapping exists yet for either, record both directions.
9. Optimized Solution
Two hash maps, one per direction, checked and updated in a single pass.
Dry run for pattern = "abba", s = "dog cat cat dog"

blocks.content: {"headers":["Position","Letter","Word","Action","Why"],"rows":[["0","a","dog","no mapping yet, record a to dog and dog to a","Neither map has an entry yet for this letter or word, so both directions are recorded fresh"],["1","b","cat","no mapping yet, record b to cat and cat to b","This is a different letter and a different word from position 0, so both maps gain a new, independent entry"],["2","b","cat","b already maps to cat, cat already maps to b, consistent","Both recorded mappings agree with what is seen now, so no conflict exists"],["3","a","dog","a already maps to dog, dog already maps to a, consistent","Both recorded mappings again agree with what is seen now, confirming the bijection holds through the whole pattern"]]}

blocks.caption: Optimized: two hash maps checked in a single pass, one per mapping direction

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single pass with constant time map operations.
Space: O(n), for the two hash maps.
Why This Works

Checking char_to_word and word_to_char before overwriting either of them, at every position, guarantees that any contradiction against an earlier commitment is caught at the exact moment it happens, since a hash map's stored value always reflects the very first mapping ever committed for that key. Because both directions are checked every time, neither a many-letters-to-one-word nor a one-letter-to-many-words violation can slip through undetected.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Check","What it catches"],"rows":[["char_to_word already set to a different word for this letter","This same letter previously mapped to a different word: violates the letter-to-word direction"],["word_to_char already set to a different letter for this word","This same word previously mapped to a different letter: violates the word-to-letter direction"]]}

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: zip(pattern, words), or iterating by index, pairs each letter with its corresponding word directly, since the two sequences are meant to correspond position by position.

Both lookup checks happen before either map is updated for the current position, so the check always compares against a mapping established at some strictly earlier position, never against the value about to be written.
The maps are only updated once both checks have passed, meaning a position is only "recorded" after being confirmed conflict-free.
The length check up front avoids ever attempting to pair mismatched-length sequences.

blocks.text: 10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Time","Space","Notes"],"rows":[["Brute force (all-pairs recheck)","O(n squared)","O(n)","Every position is compared against every other position, including itself"],["Optimized (two hash maps, single pass)","O(n)","O(n)","Each position checked and recorded exactly once, against both direction maps"]]}

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

This problem is a clean demonstration of enforcing a bijection, a mapping that is one to one in both directions, using two hash maps, a pattern that reappears in isomorphism style problems comparing two sequences element by element.
Common mistakes

items: Checking the mapping in only one direction (letter to word), which misses the case where two different letters incorrectly map to the same word, a violation only visible from the word-to-letter direction.

Forgetting to check that pattern and the word list are the same length before comparing them position by position, which can cause an index-out-of-range error or silently ignore extra elements depending on the language.
Updating a map entry before checking its previous value, which would overwrite the very evidence needed to detect a conflict at that position.

blocks.text: Edge cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["A pattern with repeated letters mapping consistently to the same repeated word","Correctly returns true, since both maps agree at every repeated occurrence"],["More words in s than letters in pattern, or vice versa","Rejected immediately based on length alone, since no bijection can exist between sequences of different lengths"]]}

blocks.text: Interview tips

items: Explicitly state why two maps are needed instead of one, since this is the detail most likely to be tested with a follow up question or a tricky test case.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Is there a one-to-one correspondence, bijection, or isomorphism between these two sequences" points toward two hash maps, one per direction, checked together at every position, not just one direction alone.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would you solve Isomorphic Strings, which asks the same style of question about two strings instead of a pattern and a word list? The identical two-hash-map technique applies directly, just mapping characters to characters in both directions instead of characters to words.

What if the words in s could repeat in ways that make the split ambiguous, such as multiple consecutive spaces? The splitting step would need to handle that explicitly, such as collapsing repeated whitespace, before the same bijection check can be applied.

Could this be solved with a single hash map instead of two? Only by encoding both directions into one combined structure, such as mapping each letter to a unique integer ID assigned to each new word and separately checking those IDs are used consistently, which is more complex without a genuine advantage over the clear two-map approach.

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Same two-hash-map bijection enforcement as the classic Isomorphic Strings problem, essentially the same technique applied one level up, characters mapping to entire words instead of to other characters.
Same "check both directions of a claimed one-to-one relationship" discipline needed anywhere a mapping must be verified as a true bijection, not just a function in one direction.
Same "record on first sight, then check consistency on every later sight" technique as Ransom Note's frequency counting, just tracking an identity mapping instead of a quantity.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n squared) time, O(n) space.
Optimized: O(n) time, O(n) space.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: Bijection verification with two hash maps, one per mapping direction
Core Idea: A true one-to-one correspondence between pattern's letters and s's words requires checking both letter-to-word and word-to-letter consistency at every position
Time: O(n)
Space: O(n), for the two hash maps
Most Important Observation: Checking only one direction of a claimed bijection can silently miss violations that only appear from the other direction
Interview Difficulty: Easy to Medium
One-line memory trick: Two maps, both directions, checked together
